The Potential of Biophilic Design
and Nature to Improve Health, Creativity
and Well-Being
Isabelle A. K. Sjövall and Hugo J. Spiers
Abstract The human brain evolved in adaptive response to natural environments.
However, urbanisation has led to the majority of humanity now living in cities,
which differ profoundly from the landscape in which our species originated. At the
same time, mental health conditions are increasing rapidly worldwide. Studies sug-
gest that city living impacts brain function and structure, activates the stress response
to a greater extent, and increases the risk of multiple mental health conditions.
Recently, the close-to-nature concepts of biophilia and biophilic design have
emerged as a potential approach to counteract these challenges. They may play a
pivotal role in achieving the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals. Here,
we explore the potential of biophilic design to balance urban stressors, protect men-
tal health and support sustainable living on a global scale.
Keywords Biophilic Design · Sustainability · Mental Health · Creativity ·
Wellbeing
Introduction
Mental health is a crucial component of overall health and quality of life (Prince
et al., 2007). Mental health conditions are rising worldwide and are now considered
leading contributors to global disability, ranging from anxiety and depression to
severe mental illnesses such as schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder (Patel et al.,
2018; World Health Organization, 2022). Recently, interest in mental health has
increased due to its vital role in reaching the United Nations’ Sustainable
Development Goals. For example, the goals aimed at good health and well-being,
reduced inequalities and sustainable cities and communities (United Nations, 2023).

Mental health is considerably interconnected with direct and indirect diverse bio-
logical, psychological and environmental influences and is significantly associated
with overall health and quality of life (Prince et al., 2007; van den Bosch & Meyer-
Lindenberg, 2019) (➔ chapter “The CITY & the PSYCHE—A Chronology” by
Mehran, Kluge and Adli). Mental health can be defined as the absence of mental
disorders, and additionally, the ability to deal with normal stresses of life, acknowl-
edge one’s strengths and abilities, productive work and contribute to society (World
Health Organization, 2022). Although mental health is multifaceted and complex,
with many confounding variables, one fundamental factor impacting behaviour,
stress levels and mental health is the surrounding living environment (Clemenson
et al., 2015; Evans, 2003). While the world around us has developed at a rapid pace
with vast urbanisation and digitalisation, the human brain has not changed signifi-
cantly in this period. For more than 99 percent of our species’ history, humans
developed an adaptive response to natural environments, not built or engineered
ones (Kellert & Calabrese, 2015). However, now more than 50 percent of the world’s
population lives in cities, a number expected to reach 70 percent by the year 2050
(Richie & Roser, 2018). It is clear that the urban environments in which the majority
of humanity lives today stand in stark contrast to the natural environments in which
our brains have evolved (Kühn et al., 2021).
Despite their challenges, cities also offer multiple advantages such as proximity
to healthcare, work, education and culture (Hartig et al., 2014). Epidemiological
studies have also linked city living to better overall health and longer life expec-
tancy compared to rural inhabitants (Cross et al., 2021; Engemann et al., 2019). At
the same time, city dwelling has been associated with increased amygdala activity
(Lederbogen et al., 2011; Sudimac et al., 2022), cumulative environmental stress-
ors, and a significantly higher risk of mental health conditions, such as anxiety,
depression, psychosis and schizophrenia (Haddad et al., 2015; Lederbogen et al.,
2011; Reichert et al., 2020; Sundquist et al., 2004). Additionally, emerging evidence
suggests that urban living may alter brain structure and function (Kühn et al., 2017,
2020; Lederbogen et al., 2011). However, the underlying mechanisms remain
unclear.
Urban environments tend to activate the human stress response to a greater extent
than rural, natural settings (Abbott, 2012; Iglesias-Carrasco et al., 2020), with alter-
ations in the responsiveness of brain regions involved in emotion regulation, such as
the amygdala and anterior cingulate cortex (Lederbogen et al., 2011; Sudimac et al.,
2022). These findings are concerning, as prolonged stress may influence both the
onset and severity of multiple mental health conditions (Marin et al., 2011; Mariotti,
2015). Linking to urban environments, one possible underlying explanation may be
the vast and constant amount of stimuli city environments expose the brain and
body to. As a result, the cumulative burden of stressors may lead to cognitive and
allostatic overload, which in turn may alter the homeostatic balance over time
(Abbott, 2012; Isaksson, 2015; Lambert et al., 2015; McEwen, 2004; Ulrich et al.,
1991). In sum, there appear to be both advantages and disadvantages of urban expo-
sure on health and wellbeing (Abbott, 2012; Hartig & Kahn, 2016). Exploring both
specific mechanisms and collective forces behind risk and resilience factors

impacting mental health and wellbeing is therefore pivotal for the development of
future urban environments for the global population. Research is critically needed
to pinpoint and empirically establish these factors and how they relate to creating a
better balance.
The Potential of Biophilic Design
One approach to exploring how cities impact health is attempting to identify which
features of the environment might operate as protective factors, helping to lower
stress and support mental and physical health. One appealing example is the pres-
ence of greenspace and close-to-nature characteristics known as biophilic design
(Barbiero & Berto, 2021; Hartig & Kahn, 2016; Kaplan, 1995; Kellert et al., 2011;
Kühn et al., 2017; Lindal & Hartig, 2013). Biophilic design has emerged from bio-
philia, a concept first introduced by Erich Fromm and later popularised by Edward
O. Wilson, defined as ‘the love of life and of all that is alive’ or ‘the tendency of
humans to focus on and to affiliate with nature’ (Fromm, 1964, 1973; Wilson, 1986).
Biophilic design involves direct or indirect close-to-nature elements, such as
colours, patterns, greenness, motives, lighting, sounds and natural tactile materials,
such as for example wood.
In recent years, a growing body of research has acknowledged the important
potential of biophilic design as a tool for counteracting stressors and supporting
mental health. The findings range from improvements in mood, memory, positive
affect and happiness, to cognitive performance, creativity, recovery and well-being
(Bolten & Barbiero, 2020; Bratman et al., 2019; Gillis & Gatersleben, 2015; Kellert,
2018; Mostajeran et al., 2023; Stenfors et al., 2019; Ulrich, 1984; Van Hedger et al.,
2019; Wijesooriya & Brambilla, 2021). Bringing these findings together, it is tempt-
ing to consider future possibilities and positive outcomes that may emerge from
making more conscious design choices. Can biophilic design create healthier cities,
homes, schools, hospitals and workplaces, helping to better balance risk and resil-
ience factors in future living environments?
Our Approach
In this chapter, we consider the available literature, focusing on how biophilia and
biophilic design affect humans psychologically and physiologically linked to men-
tal health and creative cognition. Furthermore, we aim to identify the key features
of biophilic design and suggest new ideas for future research to further advance the
field. In addition, we propose our vision of how biophilic design qualities can be
implemented to shape symbiotic spaces in the real world with the intention of sup-
porting health and sustainable living in future built environments.

Method
A comprehensive search of peer-reviewed papers was completed through PubMed,
Google Scholar, ScienceDirect and Cochrane, based on the key terms; ‘Biophilia’,
‘Biophilic Design’, ‘Mental health’, ‘Creativity‘, ‘Built Environment’. High-impact
journals, including Nature, Science and The Lancet, were independently searched.
The included articles were selected due to their relevance, suitability and impact,
with careful consideration to match the aims of this chapter. A limited number of
books have been included, motivated by their originality and unique contribution to
the field. Chat GPT and Gemini have been used to generate ideas, with care taken to
consider for confabulations (e.g. no facts listed trusted).
Background and Overview: Biophilia and Biophilic Design
The biophilia hypothesis suggests that humans have an innate connection with
nature. Biophilic design can be defined as design elements inspired by nature, typi-
cally involving colours, patterns, greenness, sounds, smells, fractals, lighting,
motives and natural materials, such as wood (Barbiero & Berto, 2021; Kellert et al.,
2011). From a neurobiological and evolutionary perspective, the biophilic design
concept is appealing as the brain evolved in adaptive response to natural environ-
ments, why a universal preference for close-to-nature characteristics in architecture
and design seems logical.
A Dose of Nature
In recent years, there has been increasing interest in biophilia and biophilic design,
as a growing number of studies have demonstrated positive psychological and phys-
iological health outcomes associated with nature exposure. Important examples
include reduced stress levels; improved immune function, memory, lower blood
pressure, slower epigenetic ageing, better sleep quality and quantity, as well as
increased performance, creativity, cognition, mood and well-being (Beukeboom
et al. 2012; Kim et al., 2023; Li, 2010, Li et al., 2009, 2011; McCoy & Evans, 2002;
Ulrich, 1992). These findings are interesting since very few other interventions have
the same powerful potential, as nature seems to have multiple domains related to
human health outcomes. The next section explores the key elements and character-
istics of biophilic design and its various effects on physical and mental health.

Key Elements of Biophilic Design: A Multisensory Approach
Biophilic design is a multifaceted concept that consists of several separate elements.
Each element has a close-to-nature look and feel and has been independently linked
to positive physical and mental health outcomes. Here, ten core characteristics of
biophilic design are presented (Fig. 1).
Natural Materials
Recent developments in the field of ecological sustainability have led to a renewed
interest in wooden materials. From a holistic perspective, it is interesting to consider
the properties of wood connected to human health, as a growing body of research
has found positive effects on mood, cognition and creativity (Beute & De Kort,
2014; Bhatta et al., 2017; McCoy & Evans, 2002; Strobel et al., 2017; Vavrinsky
et al., 2019). A clear example is natural materials, such as wood, which provide a
multisensory connection with nature (Kellert, 2016). Wooden materials have been
found to reduce stress and cortisol levels, lower heart rate and blood pressure and
enhance well-being (Beute & de Kort, 2014; Fell, 2010; Kotradyova et al., 2019;
Tsunetsugu et al., 2007).

260 I. A. K. Sjövall and H. J. Spiers
Colours
Colours may play a pivotal role in inducing psychological and physiological states
(Elliot & Maier, 2014). Green and blue spaces (e.g. foliage and water) have been
found to support cognitive function and mental well-being (White et al., 2021), and
Lichtenfeld et al. (2012) proposed that the green colour could facilitate creative
performance. Other research by Mehta and Zhu (2009) suggested a link between the
colour blue and enhanced creative task performance. These studies suggest a benefi-
cial link between natural nuances (reminiscent of blue skies, water, green plants and
vegetation). Some studies have proposed that viewing blue or green may be particu-
larly beneficial for creative performance (Lichtenfeld et al., 2012; Mehta & Zhu,
2009; Küller et al., 2009). Another well-studied colour is red, a poignant colour in
biology and nature often associated with arousal and warning signals. For example,
in poisonous reptiles and insects (Stevens & Ruxon, 2012), perhaps most impor-
tantly, the colour of blood is closely connected to life and death (Elliot & Maier,
2014). Other nuances have not been empirically examined. Although the green/
blue/red findings seem well aligned with Kellert’s (2008) search into biophilic
design, which emphasises that colours often resonate with our evolutionary predis-
position towards nature.
Shapes
Organic curvilinear shapes may have originated from an evolutionary mechanism
(Bar & Neta, 2006). In recent years, research has explored the cognitive and neural
mechanisms supporting preference for natural and organic shapes (Bar and Neta,
2006, 2007; Leder et al., 2011; Vartanian et al., 2013; Bertamini et al., 2016).
Vartanian et al. (2013) demonstrated that curvilinear forms activated the medial
orbitofrontal cortex, a region involved in emotional processing (Etkin et al., 2011).
Moreover, work by Ramachandran and Hirstein (1999) related to aesthetic appre-
ciation suggests that organic forms can induce enhanced pleasure responses, high-
lighting our biological preference for natural shapes and forms.
Fractal Patterns
Fractals are self-repeating structures found in nature (Taylor, 2021). These patterns
are prevalent throughout natural scenery and can be found everywhere in nature and
biology, for example on trees, leaves, flowers and coastlines (Taylor et al., 2005).
Interestingly, neurons also use fractal geometry to enhance network connectivity
(Smith et al., 2021). Research using electroencephalogram (EEG) recording has
reported modulation in alpha oscillations in the frontal lobes and the highest beta
oscillations in the parietal regions (Hagerhall et al., 2015). These findings indicate a

complex interplay between neural networks when experiencing these patterns, and
the outcomes have demonstrated both states of relaxation and elevated attention
(Hagerhall et al., 2008, 2015). Other studies have found a reduction in physiological
stress and enhanced rehabilitation when exposed to fractal patterns in art and archi-
tecture (Taylor et al., 2011; Vaz et al., 2020). Fractals could be connected to evolu-
tionary developed patterns aesthetic appreciation. Implementing fractal patterns in
architecture and design may therefore have significant potential for future built
environments and cities.
Tactile Textures
The sensory experience of touch has a fundamental impact on human physiological,
cognitive and emotional responses (Jansson-Boyd, 2011). Perhaps not surprising, as
touch provides us with important sensory information and contact with the external
world (Barnett, 1972; Gallace, 2012; Gallace & Spence, 2008; Gallace & Spence,
2010). Positive touch responses can stimulate the release of oxytocin, a key chemi-
cal for social bonding and relaxation (McGlone et al., 2014; Uvnäs-Moberg et al.,
2015; Yu et al., 2022). Studies have shown that tactile touch can lead to significantly
lower anxiety levels and increased resilience to stress. The underlying mechanism
is suggested to be a reduction in noradrenalin requirements (Henricson et al., 2008;
Dagnino-Subiabre, 2022). Gallace and Spence’s (2010) research further exemplifies
this argument by proposing that varied textures, especially those mimicking nature,
can significantly modify mood and overall well-being. Natural tactile materials pro-
mote sensory stimulation and provide cognitive, physiological and psychological
benefits.
Light
Ranging from natural daylight to artificial lighting sources, light has profound
implications for human health and performance. The background is the importance
of light for circadian rhythms, as this system orchestrates complicated chemical bal-
ances in the brain and the body. Natural daylight has been associated with improved
alertness and enhanced cognitive functioning (Choi & Suk, 2016). In contrast, warm
light, mimicking sunsets or candlelight, may induce relaxation (Inagaki &
Eisenberger, 2013). Exposure timings, colour temperature and strength can influ-
ence mood, productivity and overall health (Choi & Suk, 2016; Inagaki &
Eisenberger, 2013). Furthermore, Rea et al. (2010) highlight the importance of
lighting compatible with circadian rhythms, underscoring its influence on sleep and
health. In recent years a growing interest in human-centric lighting (HCL) has
emerged. HCL is artificial lighting that aims to provide close-to-nature lighting, tap-
ping into natural circadian rhythms. Properly used, HCL has the potential to improve
lighting within the architecture and design process (Houser & Esposito, 2021).

262 I. A. K. Sjövall and H. J. Spiers
Greenery
Green plants are perhaps the element most associated with biophilic design. For the
past few decades, the interest in plants has surged, particularly in office design
driven primarily by the wish to boost productivity and performance. Research con-
sistently indicates that plants can improve air quality, reduce stress and improve
mood, productivity and cognitive performance (Aydogan & Cerone, 2021;
Bringslimark et al., 2007; Hall & Knuth, 2019; Raanaas et al., 2011). Kellert et al.
(2011) presented a comprehensive overview of advantages of biophilia in office set-
tings, proposing that the integration of nature may enhance productivity. Later stud-
ies support this perspective. One good example is the work by Lei et al. (2021) The
study focuses on identifying the optimal greenery dose for workplace well-being,
including physiological, psychological and productivity aspects. A repeated-
measures experiment was carried out using green coverage ratios of 0%, 0.2%, 5%,
12% and 20%. Health and productivity were measured through questionnaires,
tasks, alongside eye tracking to test visual engagement with greenery. The findings
indicate that while all levels of greenery improved work performance, only 12% and
20% green coverage ratios significantly enhanced physiological brain activities.
Interestingly, a 20% coverage ratio was identified as overwhelming, making the
12% greenery ratio the recommended dose for biophilic design in office environ-
ments. This study provides valuable data for biophilic design research and practice,
identifying a potential dose–response for enhancing workplace well-being (Lei
et al., 2021). Furthermore, Kaplan (1993) underlines the importance of green and
natural elements in restorative environments. As restoration is a crucial component
for productivity and performance, it is logical that green plants are used as a natural
part of architectural design to contribute to reinforcing a healthy work environment.
Greenery may also extend to artificial plants, which may be particularly beneficial
in environments with no natural light (Beukeboom et al., 2012). On a larger scale, it
can be implemented in urban design as green roofs and facades to help improve air
quality and keep down rising temperatures linked to global warming.
Sounds
Studies have consistently shown that the sounds of nature such as animals, wind and
water, are preferred over anthropogenic sounds such as traffic and industrial noise
(Yang & Kang, 2005; Fisher, 1999). The sounds of nature such as diverse birdsong,
rustling leaves or a calm water stream can provide positive sensory stimuli to coun-
teract stressing urban sounds such as traffic noise. Research by Alvarsson et al.
(2010) found that nature sounds can reduce stress levels, restore cognitive ability
and facilitate recovery from sympathetic activation by contributing to relaxation and
well-being. Other studies have also highlighted the health advantages of auditory
stimuli to better balance city stressors by increasing recovery stress resilience, and
demonstrate that birdsongs reduced depressivity, anxiety and paranoia in healthy
participants (Gould van Praag et al. 2017; Stobbe et al., 2022). Auditory experiences

associated with nature therefore hold a therapeutic promise for architectural design
and future urban environments.
Scents
The olfactory dimension and nature’s fragrances play a profound role in biophilic
design. Incorporating natural scents within the architecture and design associated
with nature, can add richness to the multisensory experience and induce a sense of
belonging and psychological well-being (Joye & Van den Berg, 2011). Research by
Franco et al. (2017) suggests that certain natural scents, such as those from pine
trees or fresh soil, may have calming and relaxing effects, as well as reduce anxiety
and physiological stress-related biomarkers (Franco et al., 2017). Another example
of the positive effects of natural scents is phytoncides, a natural chemical released
from trees that have been found to strengthen mood and immune function (Li, 2010;
Herz, 2009). Building further on these findings, essential oils may be of benefit.
Research has found that olfactory stimulation by orange or rose oil may result in a
significant decrease in oxyhemoglobin concentration in the right prefrontal cortex,
a region linked to memory for use in speech, and in addition induce positive changes
in mood and cognitive function, as well as an increase in a comfortable and relaxed
state of mind (Gabrieli et al., 1998; Igarashi et al., 2014). Integrating the olfactory
dimension into biophilic design not only amplifies a positive atmosphere but can
also support human health and psychological well-being.
Vistas
Robust research shows that visual exposure to nature and landscapes has significant
positive outcomes that can lower stress hormones, heart rate and blood pressure, as
well as support overall health and well-being (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989). Furthermore,
these views may enhance mood, support attention restoration and activate brain
regions associated with higher cognitive functions linked to emotional regulation
(Berman et al., 2008). The therapeutic potential of natural views is also accentuated
in hospital settings due to its capacity to reduce stress and accelerate recovery
(Sternberg, 2009; Ulrich, 1984). A pioneering study by Ulrich (1984) explored
recovery records in a hospital environment. Patients who had undergone surgery
were assigned to a room either with a window facing a natural setting or a brick wall
to examine whether the view might influence recovery. The patients who were
assigned to rooms with windows with a natural scene had shorter hospital stays,
fewer negative comments in staff’s notes, and took less pain medication (Ulrich,
1984). Using nature vistas in built environments may be a fundamental component
to enhance health, recovery and well-being. Taken together, these ten key character-
istics of biophilic design show great promise and potential to support physiological
and mental health. The next section will investigate the stress response linked to the
built environment and cities (Fig. 2).

Cities, Stress and the Immune System
From an evolutionary perspective, it has been advantageous for biological organ-
isms such as humans to adapt to the surrounding environment to maintain overall
homeostasis and optimise chances of survival. Homeostasis is pivotal for physical
and mental health, defined as the process of the internal environment of a living
organism to remain steady and balanced (Romero et al., 2009; McEwen & Wingfield,
2010). Prolonged stress can cause homeostatic imbalances and ultimately result in
illness (Hoogendoorn et al., 2017). The field of neuroimmunology indicates that
chronic or repeated exposure to external or internal stressors may alter homeostatic
balance (van den Bosch & Meyer-Lindenberg, 2019). Related to these findings,
pioneering research has linked nature exposure to enhanced immune function. The
research has shown a decrease in interleukin-6 (IL-6), a key inflammatory bio-
marker, when regularly exposed to nature. Taken together, these findings demon-
strate a robust immune response suggesting that parasympathetic activation
contributes to both physical and mental equilibrium (Ulrich & Gilpin, 1999; Ulrich
et al., 2010; Li, 2010; Stenfors et al., 2019).

City as a Stressor
Linking to urban environments and city settings, it is critical to contemplate the
impact of constant exposure to various stressors, as studies suggest stress as a core
component in both the onset and symptom severity of multiple mental health condi-
tions (Abbott, 2012; Adli & Schöndorf, 2020; Sapolsky, 1999; Slavich & Irwin,
2014). The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA) is a homeostatic brain-body
system playing a fundamental part in psychological well-being and mental health.
This system is activated by both internal and external forces, including stressors
from the surrounding environment (Sapolsky et al., 2000). Activation of the HPA-
axis is initiated in the brain’s paraventricular nucleus, leading to the release of
corticotropin- releasing hormone. The hormone induces adrenocorticotropic hor-
mone from the pituitary gland into the vascular system and activates the adrenal
glands to release the glucocorticoid hormone cortisol. This system acts to regulate
daily physiological processes in the body such as respiratory rate, heart rate, glu-
cose levels and immune system response to stress, activating above-normal levels in
reaction to fight-or-flight situations (Hoogendoorn et al., 2017; Sapolsky et al.,
2000). Long-term exposure to environmental stressors can result in a state of chronic
stress and HPA dysregulation, which in turn can stimulate alterations in reward
pathways (Adam & Epel, 2007 Gold, 2015; McEwen, 2017). One potential expla-
nation for the elevated stress levels in urban environments may therefore be the
exposure to numerous and prolonged stressors, resulting in chronic stress and HPA
dysregulation (Valentine, 2023). This accumulative ‘cost’ is sometimes referred to
as allostatic load. Allostatic load indicates the cumulative physiological burden
experienced by the body as it constantly adjusts to stressors from the surrounding
environment (Sterling & Eyer, 1988). Extensive exposure to stressors can result in
allostatic overload, ultimately manifested by disturbances in various physiological
systems, including the cardiovascular, metabolic and immune systems (McEwen,
1998). As stress is a well-known mediator in many mental health conditions, this
may induce alterations in reward pathways and change serotonergic and noradren-
ergic receptors in the brain, increasing the risk of mental health conditions (Marin
et al., 2011; Mariotti, 2015). To better balance risk and resilience factors could be
essential to counteract the mental health challenges that emerge alongside rising
urbanisation.
Stress and Inflammation
Emerging evidence suggests that prolonged stress can cause chronic inflammation.
Research in recent years has linked inflammatory biomarkers to mental health con-
ditions such as anxiety, depression, psychosis and schizophrenia (Aas et al., 2014;
Aruldass et al., 2021; Bullmore, 2018; Fraguas et al., 2019; Pariante, 2017;
Yuan et al., 2019). Notably, the same illnesses are more prevalent in urban

populations (Sundquist et al., 2004; Peen et al., 2010). These findings align with
previous pioneering research by Lederbogen et al. (2011) which found that the
amygdala, part of the brain’s limbic system associated with initiating acute stress
responses, to be more active in city dwellers compared to rural dwellers (Lederbogen
et al., 2011). Moreover, individuals who took a forest walk, rather than an urban
walk, prior to fMRI scanning showed a lower amygdala response to face stimuli
(Sudimac et al., 2022). Therefore, even brief exposure to natural settings may
impact brain function in the time period immediately after exposure, supporting the
idea that short-term contact with natural settings can have a calming effect on brain
regions associated with stress response. Future health policies and urban planning
processes should address the complex interplay between the built environment,
stressors, inflammatory responses and mental health to aim to better balance these
environments with counteracting components such as green space and biophilic
design elements.
Neuroanatomical Impacts of Stress: Neuroplasticity
and Neurogenesis
Chronic stress has been associated with decreased neuroplasticity and neurogenesis,
which are two key processes for good mental health (Uchida et al., 2018).
Neuroplasticity refers to the brain’s ability to reshape in response to the external
world, and neurogenesis is defined as the brain’s capacity to form new neurons
throughout life (Clemenson et al., 2015; Pittenger & Duman, 2008; Spalding et al.,
2013). Robust research in animal models has found that environments rich in natu-
ral sensory stimuli can support both neuroplasticity and neurogenesis (Clemenson
et al., 2015; van Praag et al., 2000). In humans, it is not clear which environments
that can be enriching. However, research in recent years points at nature as one
direction in promoting these biological processes (Kühn et al., 2017, 2020). The
next section will explore these new studies and in addition, draw conclusions from
large epidemiological research linking the environment and mental health.
Green Impact on Mental Health, Brain Structure
and Brain Function
Epidemiological research by Engemann and colleagues with over 900,000 partici-
pants discovered an association between the amount of green space in one’s residen-
tial environment during childhood and the risk of developing psychiatric disorders
later in life (Engemann et al., 2019). Children growing up in environments with very
low levels of green space had an increased prevalence of up to 55% of developing
mental health disorders with other risk factors taken into account (Engemann et al.,

The Potential of Biophilic Design and Nature to Improve Health, Creativity… 267
2019). These findings are in line with earlier epidemiological studies showing an
association between time spent in cities during childhood and adolescence and a
greater risk of developing mental health disorders in adulthood (Sundquist et al.,
2004). These epidemiological studies indicate a dose-response relationship both in
terms of time and the amount of green space.
The association between green spaces and stress resilience is further exemplified
in work undertaken by Kühn et al. (2017), which identifies a significant positive
relationship between forest coverage and amygdala integrity. Additionally, differ-
ences have been observed comparing individuals exclusively raised in urban or rural
environments. Using voxel-based morphometry, the results revealed a difference in
the left hippocampal formation on group level comparing rural and city exposures.
This was positively associated with enhanced cognitive performance in a spatial
processing task (Kühn et al., 2020). These results are interesting in the context of
urban design and its potential future directions, as proximity to and exposure to
green spaces may not only encourage spatial exploration but also build stress resil-
ience and improve mental well-being in city populations.
Spatial Structure of the Environment
The spaces we visit can offer a range of affordances that help meet different needs
(Gregorians & Spiers, 2022). It has been argued humans tend to seek out environ-
ments that offer both ‘prospect’ spaces with open views, and ‘refuge’ spaces for
shelter and protection (Appleton, 1984; Dosen & Ostwald, 2016). From an evolu-
tionary perspective, these spatial preferences have optimised chances of survival by
supporting threat detection, as well as offering a safe retreat (Heft, 2010). These
spatial preferences and constructs may also be activated in contemporary contexts.
An example is negative affect when being exposed to high-rise buildings (Mazumder
et al., 2022), or the stress one might experience when getting lost in a complex
building, as this may tap into evolved neural systems that detect vulnerability to
threats in unfamiliar landscapes (Hart & Moore, 1973). These instinctual cognitive
states profoundly shape navigation and wayfinding behaviours (Golledge, 1999;
Montello, 2005; Ekstrom et al., 2018). Especially how the surrounding environment
shapes our ability to navigate (Gregorians & Spiers, 2022). To give one example;
growing up inside vs outside cities (particularly griddy cities) has an impact on
navigation abilities (Coutrot et al., 2022; Spiers et al., 2023). By testing over 380,000
participants on a virtual navigation test with ecological validity, and asking about
the home environment, findings indicate that growing up in griddy cities leads to
worse navigation performance, particularly in disorganised environments Coutrot
et al., 2018, 2019, 2022). For example, individuals growing up in a city like Buenos
Aires in Argentina, which is rather grid-like and well-structured, will on average be

The Stress of Being Lost
A key environment where being lost is commonplace is hospital environments.
Navigating large hospitals can be a very challenging and stressful experience
because of the practical complexity of healthcare spaces and the typical absence of
indoor digital map guidance. Additionally, the look-and-feel of the hospital environ-
ment is often sterile with few visual variations which makes it even more difficult to
navigate. Moreover, poor wayfinding and disorientation are among the first core
symptoms of Alzheimer’s dementia which is particularly problematic in hospitals
(Coughlan et al., 2018). This combination can lead to stress and negative experi-
ences among patients and staff. An appealing example of how green spaces could be
used to enhance wayfinding is an experiment by Jiang et al. (2022). By using
immersive virtual reality and high-definition virtual models of hospitals, partici-
pant’s mood, wayfinding performance and spatial experience were examined in hos-

better wayfinding performance for the environments with visable green spaces,
measured by shorter walking distance, less sign viewing, and fewer stops, more
efficient route selection, and less time spent on finding the correct destination.

Awe and Creative Thinking
Building further on this body of research, it is interesting to explore the connection
between nature, awe and creativity. Nature exposure has been found to activate the
parasympathetic nervous system and stimulate an ‘at ease’ state, which promotes
‘mental equilibrium’ and creative thinking (Tversky, 2019). Awe is a relatively
new concept in empirical research which can be described as a feeling of connected-
ness and presence with something greater than oneself, accompanied by wonder or
fascination (Shiota et al., 2007). Awe experiences can originate from various stim-
uli, such as impressive and beautiful architecture, or breath-taking natural views or
landscapes (Zhao et al., 2018). Research has also found a link between awe and
activation of the default mode network in the brain, a neural network associated
with rest, mind-wandering, introspection and daydreaming, a network crucial for
cognitive flexibility and creative thinking (Andrews-Hanna, 2012; Beaty et al.,
2015; Buckner et al., 2008; Stellar et al., 2018). Relating to these findings, Tversky
(2019) suggests that our spatial and navigational thinking, which is often stimulated
to a greater extent in nature and natural settings, may positively influence abstract
thoughts and creative thinking. Implementing biophilic design and natural elements
may contribute to the enhanced interplay between the parasympathetic nervous sys-
tem, the default mode network, and creativity (Mostarejan et al., 2023).
Biophilia, Biophobia?
While a growing body of research indicates the benefits of biophilia and biophilic
design, contrasting studies on biophobia somewhat challenge this idea. The concept
of biophobia suggests that humans evolved to react with instinctive fear and caution
of certain elements in the natural world that present potential threats (Ohman &
Mineka, 2001) Although empirical studies on biophobia are relatively scarce and
evidence is less robust compared to biophilia, the research indicates an innate pre-
disposition for reluctant, negative or biophobic responses to some natural stimuli
such for example snakes, spiders, certain plants and heights (Ulrich, 1993; Wertz &
Wynn, 2014). Studies have explored autonomic nervous system markers for differ-
ent types of natural stimuli which indicate different responses to geometric figures
and flowers, compared to snakes and spiders (Ohman et al., 2001; Ohman 2009;
Sabatinelli et al., 2005). From a neurobiological perspective, this is logical, as it is

crucial to distinguish risk-relevant and non-risk-relevant stimuli in natural wild
environments. Avoiding snakes and other dangerous animals is crucial to enhance
chances for survival, while non-risk-relevant natural stimuli may indicate environ-
mental richness, biodiversity and food. To summarise, separating risk-relevant and
non-risk-relevant natural stimuli has been, and still is, evolutionary advantageous to
optimise human survival.
Conclusion
By 2050, 70 percent of the world’s population is estimated to live in urban environ-
ments (Richie & Roser, 2018). Cities offer many opportunities such as proximity to
work, education and healthcare (Hartig et al., 2014). However, in parallel with rapid
urbanisation, mental health conditions are rising (Patel et al., 2018; World Health
Organization, 2022). Empirical evidence suggests that exposure to nature can help
to counteract these challenges as nature is linked to multiple psychological and
physiological pathways, and is associated with mental health, such as restoration,
physical activity, and social interaction, as well as immune function, brain develop-
ment and cognition (Beukeboom et al. 2012; Engemann et al., 2019; Goldy & Piff,
2020; Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989; Kaplan et al., 1989; Kim et al., 2023; Kühn et al.,
2017, 2020; Li, 2010, Li et al., 2009, 2011; McCoy & Evans, 2002; Oppezzo &
Schwartz, 2014; Ulrich et al., 1991; Ulrich, 1992). As a result of emerging empirical
evidence in scientific research, design disciplines outside academia have started to
acknowledge the potential of implementing biophilic characteristics in architectural
design and built environments (Camargo et al., 2018). Recently, there has been a
strong interest among architects, designers, developers and decision-makers to
implement and apply biophilic design to the built environment beyond green plants.
Symbiotic Spaces and their Implications
for Sustainable Development
The twenty-first century is marked by the escalating urgency to navigate the nexus
between human health, ecological protection and economic sustainability. Achieving
the Sustainable Development Goals requires innovative solutions and urgent action
on a global scale. At the centre of this discussion is the potential of biophilic design
as a prospective tool in counteracting these challenges. In the context of sustainable
development, the concept of symbiotic spaces stands out as an appealing alterna-
tive. The concept brings together natural and man-made elements creating a cycle
of mutual benefit. This approach not only nurtures the environment but may also
support human health, well-being and economic growth. Thus, there is vast

Critical Evaluation of the Biophilia Hypothesis: Gaps
in Existing Research
While the concept of biophilia has a robust theoretical foundation, the multimodal
impact of biophilic design in modern, real-world built environments and potential
dose effects needs to be further examined. There may be scenarios or situations
where it is less effective and its use needs to be carefully considered (Fitzgerald,
2023. Previous research has mainly originated from fields such as environmental
psychology, sociology and anthropology. These studies generally explore how
interaction with nature can positively affect human well-being. However, much of
this research has relied on self-reported metrics, such as questionnaires and surveys,
which are vulnerable to subjective bias.
Furthermore, epidemiological studies have correlated urban living with poorer
mental health outcomes. These studies often use registry-based research methods,
which provide large sample sizes and strong statistical power; however, they are
insufficient for understanding causal relationships between architectural design
characteristics and mental health. This limitation indicates a significant opportunity
for future research to explore causal links between the built environment and men-
tal health.
A limited number of MRI studies (➔ chapter “Interplay Between the Physical
Environment and the Human Brain: A Review of MRI Research” by Beyer et al.) in
recent years have identified alterations in stress-responses, and brain structure and
function, linking neural changes to greenspace exposure. These studies provide a
worthy foundation for further research in the search for causal elements in city envi-
ronments that may mediate mental health outcomes. Although MRI is still consid-
ered the gold standard within neuroscientific research, recent advances in
neuroscience offer promising opportunities for complementing objective measures
to the existing field of research. For example, novel neurotechnology such as mobile
EEG (➔ chapter “EEG for the Study of Environmental Neuroscience”, by Grassini)
and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) create interesting new opportu-
nities to measure brain activity in real-world environments (e.g. Burgess et al.,
2022). When combined with other physiological biomarkers, like smartwatches and
body sensors, these technologies and methods have significant potential to add
objective qualitative measures to advance the research field. Most studies have pri-
marily focused on the psychological and physiological benefits of exposure to
nature and green space. Future research could explore other biophilic aspects of
urban environments, such as how architectural design provides access to daylight,
encourages movement and fosters social connections.

A clear gap in existing research is the predominant focus on the visual system. A
multisensory approach, considering all senses—touch, sight, hearing, smell, and
taste—could provide a more comprehensive and realistic perspective that is closely
connected to real-world environments. Additional research is also needed to exam-
ine social and cross-cultural differences when examining biophilia and close-to-
nature experiences, as these may vary. The current body of research has mainly
focused on Western populations, often overlooking the role of socio-cultural factors
in human-nature experiences and interactions.
Another limitation within biophilic research is the wide definition of biophilia
and biophilic design. Clearer definitions and a standardised framework may enable
more rigorous research evaluating the theoretical and empirical validity of biophilia
and biophilic design. A more nuanced and multifaceted approach could clarify the
complex mechanisms behind the potential impact of biophilic design on human
cognition, behaviour and mental health, and provide a more holistic perspective.
Vision and Future Directions
More research is needed to gain solid empirical grounding within this field. Applying
an interdisciplinary approach integrating insights from multiple scientific disci-
plines could offer new possibilities for more comprehensive and refined research.
Such an approach is essential for a nuanced understanding of the complex mecha-
nisms behind biophilic design‘s impact on human cognition, behaviour and mental
health. Incorporating biophilic design at different scales in future cities, buildings,
and interiors by microdosing natural elements could cumulatively provide signifi-
cant improvements for human health. Implementing biophilic design in future
architecture, design, and infrastructure therefore has the potential to create a holistic
whole greater than the sum of its parts.
